description: Phase 1 schema sample. These items are editorial examples and do not count toward production category floors.

items.title: Correlate framework fingerprints across independent response signals
items.objective: Identify likely server-side frameworks without treating a single mutable banner as proof.
prerequisites: At least two in-scope public responses
steps: Record response headers, cookie names, generated markup, asset paths, and error-page structure
Compare at least two independent signals against official framework behavior
Record the result as a hypothesis and note conflicting evidence

examples.response:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: session=REDACTED; Secure; HttpOnly
examples.note: A generic cookie name alone does not identify a framework.

items.manipulate: A harmless path or Accept header only when another response is needed for comparison
items.secure_behavior: Responses minimize unnecessary product detail; any residual signals do not by themselves expose an exploitable condition.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A precise obsolete component version is consistently exposed and can be tied to a reachable vulnerable feature.
items.validation: Confirm with multiple independent signals and verify any claimed version against an official vendor source before raising risk.
false_positives: Reverse proxies can add or rewrite product headers
Cookie names and default paths can be customized or copied across frameworks
items.impact: Reliable fingerprinting can focus later testing; it is normally an observation unless combined with a demonstrated vulnerable component.
evidence: Redacted response excerpts showing each signal

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Fingerprint Web Application Framework

items.remediation: Suppress unnecessary product/version disclosures and keep reachable components supported; do not rely on banner removal as a vulnerability fix.

items.title: Reject unsupported HTTP methods consistently across routing layers
items.objective: Determine whether alternate HTTP methods bypass routing, authentication, caching, or action controls.
prerequisites: A representative endpoint
Permission to send non-destructive alternate methods
steps: Capture the normal method and response for a representative endpoint
Send OPTIONS to understand declared method support
Repeat the request with one unsupported method while preserving all other inputs
Compare status, body, side effects, and upstream headers

examples.response:
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: GET, POST

items.manipulate: The HTTP request method only
items.secure_behavior: Unsupported methods are rejected consistently, and safe methods cannot invoke state changes.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An alternate method reaches functionality or data that the intended method cannot access, or performs an unintended state change.
items.validation: Reproduce with a control request and verify server-side state rather than relying only on a different status code.
false_positives: OPTIONS may be intentionally enabled for CORS
A framework-generated 200 response may not indicate that endpoint logic executed
items.impact: A verified method-based bypass can expose protected functions or permit unauthorized state changes.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Test HTTP Methods

items.safety: Use methods and bodies that cannot delete or mutate production data unless the owner has provided a disposable test object.
items.remediation: Allowlist methods at each routing layer and enforce authorization and action semantics independently of method overrides.

items.title: Reject vendor and deployment default credentials
items.objective: Determine whether an exposed login accepts documented default credentials for the identified product or deployment template.
prerequisites: Explicit authorization for credential testing
A confirmed product or owner-provided default account list
steps: Confirm the login belongs to an in-scope product
Select only defaults documented by the official vendor or engagement owner
Attempt each approved credential pair once
Stop immediately on success and record the assigned privilege without exploring unrelated data

examples.request:
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: admin.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=approved-test&password=REDACTED

items.manipulate: The username and password using only an approved, bounded list
items.secure_behavior: Default accounts are disabled, renamed where appropriate, or require a unique secret before use.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A documented default pair authenticates to a deployed account.
items.validation: Confirm the authenticated identity and minimum role from non-sensitive account UI or an owner-approved identity endpoint.
false_positives: A generic redirect can return the login page without establishing a session
A test environment may intentionally contain owner-documented fixture accounts
items.impact: An attacker may gain the privileges of the default account, potentially including administrative control.
evidence: Redacted login request and authenticated identity response
Product/version basis for the attempted default

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for Default Credentials

items.safety: Use a tiny owner-approved list, respect lockout thresholds, never spray accounts, and stop after the first success.
items.remediation: Require unique secrets during provisioning and disable or rotate all vendor and template defaults before exposure.

items.title: Constrain session cookies with purpose-appropriate attributes
items.objective: Determine whether each session-bearing cookie is restricted against unnecessary transport, script, cross-site, domain, and path exposure.
prerequisites: A response that creates or refreshes an authenticated session
steps: Identify cookies that actually carry or bind the session
Record Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain, Path, prefix, and lifetime attributes
Trace where each cookie is sent during normal same-site and approved cross-site flows
Assess each absent or broad attribute against the application's real threat model
items.manipulate: Cookie delivery context in browser developer tools or a controlled request; do not alter production session values
items.secure_behavior: Session cookies use the narrowest domain/path and appropriate Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, and prefix controls without breaking required flows.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A relevant attack path exposes or transmits a session cookie because a necessary restriction is absent or too broad.
items.validation: Demonstrate the cookie's actual exposure in the affected context; do not report an attribute checklist gap alone.
false_positives: HttpOnly is irrelevant to a cookie intentionally read by trusted client code if it is not an authentication secret
SameSite=None may be required for a documented cross-site flow when paired with Secure and other CSRF defenses
items.impact: Depending on the exposed context, weak cookie scope can enable session theft, fixation support, or cross-site request abuse.
evidence: Cookie purpose and observed send contexts

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for Cookies Attributes

items.remediation: Set cookie attributes from the cookie's purpose and required browser flows, minimize scope, and avoid exposing session tokens to script.

items.title: Enforce object-level authorization on sensitive resources
items.objective: Determine whether one user can read or modify another user's object by changing its reference.
prerequisites: Two authorized test accounts with distinct objects
An object identifier in a request
steps: Create or identify one test object for each account
Capture account A's authorized request
Replay it with account B's session while changing only the object reference
Repeat separately for read and permitted mutation operations
Compare with a non-existent-object control where safe

examples.request:
GET /api/orders/10293 HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Authorization: Bearer REDACTED

items.manipulate: The object reference, such as a numeric ID, UUID, filename, slug, or opaque token
items.secure_behavior: The service denies access to objects outside the caller's permission boundary, commonly with 403 or a consistent 404.
items.vulnerable_behavior: The service returns or mutates another account's object without the required permission.
items.validation: Confirm with a second account and second object, preserving all inputs except identity and object reference; verify ownership rules with the owner.
false_positives: The object is intentionally shared or public
A caching layer replayed a prior authorized response rather than performing a fresh authorization decision
items.impact: Cross-account or cross-tenant data disclosure and unauthorized modification can break confidentiality and integrity boundaries.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for Insecure Direct Object References
API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

items.remediation: Authorize every object operation server-side against the authenticated principal, action, object, and tenant rather than trusting identifier secrecy.

items.title: Detect SQL injection with paired low-impact response controls
items.objective: Determine whether untrusted input changes the structure of a backend SQL query.
prerequisites: A parameter likely used in data selection
Permission for non-destructive probes
steps: Record a stable baseline request
Submit a syntax probe and compare errors, status, body, and timing
Use paired true/false expressions appropriate to the observed input type
Repeat controls to account for caching and response variance
Stop after a minimally sufficient proof

examples.note: An error response alone is only a lead; paired controls are required.

items.manipulate: One query, path, body, header, or cookie parameter at a time
items.secure_behavior: Input remains data through parameterized queries, and malformed values receive consistent validation errors without query details.
items.vulnerable_behavior: Controlled input predictably alters query truth, timing, result shape, or database error behavior.
items.validation: Repeat a paired control/probe sequence and exclude generic validation, WAF behavior, cache variance, and application timing jitter.
false_positives: A quote can trigger ordinary input validation
A WAF block page can differ by payload without the database receiving it
Network or backend jitter can resemble a time delay
items.impact: Depending on database privilege and reachable query, exploitation can disclose or alter application data and sometimes affect the host.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for SQL Injection

items.safety: Do not extract real records, modify data, invoke operating-system features, or use heavy time delays. Stop at the least-impacting repeatable proof.
items.remediation: Use parameterized queries for every data value, constrain dynamic identifiers through allowlists, and apply least database privilege.

items.title: Verify reflected script execution in the actual output context
items.objective: Determine whether reflected input can execute script in the application's origin under a realistic browser path.
prerequisites: A reflected input
A designated test account and harmless proof marker
steps: Locate the exact reflection and classify its HTML, attribute, JavaScript, or URL context
Test whether context-appropriate encoding prevents boundary escape
Use a harmless local proof only if boundary escape is plausible
Repeat through the normal browser flow and record relevant CSP behavior
items.manipulate: The reflected parameter and only the syntax needed to test its output context
items.secure_behavior: Untrusted text is encoded for its precise output context or inserted through a safe DOM sink, so it cannot create executable syntax.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A normal application flow causes attacker-controlled script to execute in the target origin.
items.validation: Show execution with a harmless unique marker, identify the source and sink, and distinguish application reflection from proxy/browser extensions.
false_positives: Literal payload text is reflected but contextually encoded
Execution occurs only in a tester extension or proxy-rendered page
CSP blocks the tested vector and no practical bypass is established
items.impact: Exploitation can perform victim-authorized actions, read origin-accessible data, or alter trusted content, subject to victim and browser context.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for Reflected Cross Site Scripting

steps: Inspect the raw response and classify HTML text, quoted/unquoted attribute, script, style, and URL contexts before choosing syntax.
variants.notes: The same characters have different meaning in each parser context.

steps: Trace the value from URL, message, API, or storage source to its DOM sink and test the browser's parsed DOM rather than only the API response.
variants.notes: Client rendering can transform an encoded API value before insertion.

items.remediation: Apply context-specific output encoding or safe DOM APIs at the final sink, validate dangerous URL schemes, and use CSP as defense in depth.

items.title: Require an unforgeable request signal for sensitive cookie-authenticated actions
items.objective: Determine whether a third-party origin can trigger a sensitive action using the victim browser's ambient authority.
prerequisites: A reversible sensitive action on a test account
Understanding of the browser authentication transport
steps: Capture the normal state-changing request
Identify cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, Origin/Referer checks, custom headers, and SameSite behavior
Remove or alter each anti-CSRF signal independently
Reproduce the request from a controlled cross-site origin using a browser-valid request shape
Verify the state change and restore test state

examples.request:
POST /profile/email HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

email=tester%40example.test

items.manipulate: Anti-CSRF token, Origin/Referer, content type, method, and cross-site delivery context
items.secure_behavior: Sensitive actions require a validated, attacker-unavailable signal and reject cross-site requests that lack it.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A controlled third-party page can cause the authenticated browser to complete the sensitive action without informed user intent.
items.validation: Demonstrate the state change in a real browser with a test account; confirm cookie SameSite behavior for the exact navigation and method.
false_positives: A copied request works in Repeater but cannot be emitted cross-site by a browser
The response is 200 but the action is rejected or requires reauthentication
Authorization uses a header token not automatically sent by the browser
items.impact: An attacker can induce victim-authorized state changes, with impact determined by the affected action and victim privilege.
evidence: Cookie and token attributes with secrets redacted

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for Cross Site Request Forgery

steps: Build a cross-site form or navigation that matches a request shape the browser can emit and observe whether ambient cookies are attached.
variants.notes: SameSite=Lax generally excludes cross-site POST but navigation and browser details still matter.

steps: Determine whether the JWT is held in an ambient cookie or explicitly attached as an Authorization header before spending time on browser request forgery.
variants.notes: A bearer token attached only by application code usually lowers classic CSRF applicability; token storage introduces separate risks.

items.safety: Use a reversible action and designated test account. Do not submit payments, invitations, deletions, or privileged changes without explicit per-action approval.
items.remediation: Require validated anti-CSRF tokens or equivalent origin-bound signals for sensitive ambient-credential requests, combined with appropriate SameSite cookies and reauthentication for critical actions.

items.title: Prevent server-side execution of uploaded content
items.objective: Determine whether uploaded test content can be interpreted as server-side code when retrieved or processed.
prerequisites: An authorized upload feature
An inert owner-approved canary file
A disposable test object
steps: Document allowed type, extension, size, storage, and retrieval behavior
Upload an inert canary with a mismatched but non-executable type declaration
Observe server-assigned name, response headers, and storage origin
Confirm that retrieval is treated as data and cannot select an executable handler

examples.request:
POST /uploads HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=BOUNDARY

--BOUNDARY
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="canary.txt"
Content-Type: text/plain

WAPT_CANARY
--BOUNDARY--

items.manipulate: Filename, declared media type, file signature, retrieval path, and processing route using inert content
items.secure_behavior: Uploads are stored outside executable paths, receive server-generated names, are type/size constrained, and are served as inert data from an isolated origin where appropriate.
items.vulnerable_behavior: The platform routes attacker-controlled uploaded content through a server-side executable handler or unsafe processor.
items.validation: Use an inert canary or owner-provided non-destructive test handler; do not upload a command shell or execute operating-system commands.
false_positives: A file extension is accepted but served with inert content handling
Client-side validation is absent while robust server-side controls still reject or isolate the file
items.impact: Confirmed server-side execution can lead to application or host compromise under the service account's privileges.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Test Upload of Unexpected File Types

items.safety: Never upload a web shell, malware, polyglot with active content, or destructive file. Use inert canaries, clean them up, and stop if unexpected execution occurs.
items.remediation: Store uploads outside executable roots, generate names server-side, validate content and size, isolate serving, and disable execution in upload storage.

items.title: Reject unauthorized object properties in update requests
items.objective: Determine whether API consumers can write sensitive object properties that the action does not intend to expose.
prerequisites: A writable API object owned by a test account
A candidate server-managed or privileged property
steps: Capture an authorized create or update request
Compare documented writable fields with fields returned by read responses
Add one candidate server-managed field without changing legitimate fields
Retrieve the object through a fresh request and compare authorization effects
Restore the object if any state changed

examples.request:
PATCH /api/users/me HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer REDACTED

{"displayName":"Tester","role":"admin"}

items.manipulate: One undocumented, read-only, privileged, ownership, tenant, workflow, or pricing property
items.secure_behavior: Each action binds an explicit allowlist of writable properties and independently authorizes sensitive field changes.
items.vulnerable_behavior: The API persists or acts on a property the caller is not authorized to set.
items.validation: Read the object through a fresh request and confirm a security-relevant state or authorization change; a silently accepted JSON key is insufficient.
false_positives: The parser accepts but ignores the extra property
The account is legitimately authorized to set the tested property
A response echoes input without persisting it
items.impact: Depending on the property, exploitation can cause privilege escalation, tenant reassignment, pricing changes, or integrity loss.
evidence: Caller role and property authorization rule

references.title: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization

items.remediation: Bind explicit per-action data transfer objects or field allowlists and enforce field-level authorization before persistence.

items.title: Bound GraphQL query cost across aliases and nested fields
items.objective: Determine whether GraphQL query controls limit expensive nested, aliased, batched, or high-cardinality operations.
prerequisites: A confirmed GraphQL endpoint
Owner-approved resource and request ceilings
steps: Measure a small valid query as a baseline
Increase one cost dimension gradually within the approved ceiling
Test whether aliases, fragments, batching, or pagination can bypass the same limit
Record rejection behavior and recovery without pursuing service degradation

examples.request:
POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"query":"query { viewer { id } }"}

items.manipulate: Query depth, field count, aliases, batch count, page size, and resolver combinations one dimension at a time
items.secure_behavior: The service applies authenticated and anonymous cost budgets consistently and returns a controlled rejection before excessive work occurs.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A modest request bypasses limits and triggers disproportionate backend work, cost, or sustained availability impact.
items.validation: Correlate request shape with owner-approved telemetry or stable response evidence; latency alone is not enough to claim resource exhaustion.
false_positives: One cold-cache query is slow but subsequent controls are normal
A query is syntactically large but resolvers short-circuit without costly work
items.impact: Insufficient query cost controls can permit resource exhaustion or unexpected infrastructure cost.
tools: GraphQL IDE approved by the owner

references.title: OWASP ASVS 5.0.0
GraphQL API vulnerabilities

items.safety: Agree on a strict request and duration ceiling. Increase cost one small step at a time, avoid recursive/deep exhaustion payloads, and stop on elevated latency or errors.
items.remediation: Apply parser limits, cost analysis, depth/amount limits, pagination ceilings, timeouts, and per-principal resource budgets across all query transports.

items.title: Enforce a server-selected allowlist of JWT signature algorithms
items.objective: Determine whether token verification trusts attacker-controlled algorithm metadata or accepts unsigned or incorrectly keyed tokens.
prerequisites: A JWT issued to a designated test account
Permission to submit modified tokens
steps: Decode the test token locally and record its declared algorithm and key identifier
Change a harmless claim and confirm the original signature then fails
Test only the approved algorithm-confusion cases relevant to the observed verifier
Confirm acceptance or rejection at a non-destructive identity endpoint

examples.request:
GET /api/me HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...REDACTED

items.manipulate: JWT header algorithm/key metadata, signature, and one harmless test-account claim
items.secure_behavior: The verifier selects an expected algorithm and key from trusted configuration and rejects none, mismatched families, malformed signatures, and untrusted key references.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A token with an invalid, absent, or attacker-produced signature is accepted as authenticated or receives changed privileges.
items.validation: Use a fresh control token, prove a security-relevant server decision, and exclude endpoints that merely decode without authenticating the token.
false_positives: A token debugger decodes a token without verifying it
An endpoint returns generic public data regardless of token validity
The server accepts a test token through a separate documented trust path
items.impact: A verifier bypass can permit identity impersonation or privilege escalation up to any accepted claim set.
evidence: Redacted original and modified token headers/claims
Verifier response at a safe identity endpoint

references.title: RFC 8725: JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

items.safety: Modify only a designated test account token and use a read-only identity endpoint; do not impersonate real users or access their data.
items.remediation: Configure expected algorithms and keys server-side, reject none and cross-family confusion, validate key references, and use a maintained JOSE library.

items.title: Match OAuth redirect URIs exactly to the registered client allowlist
items.objective: Determine whether an authorization server accepts redirect URI variations that can deliver authorization responses to an unintended destination.
prerequisites: An owner-approved OAuth client and test identity
A controlled callback origin if redirect testing is authorized
steps: Capture a normal authorization request and registered callback
Change one URI component at a time: scheme, host, port, path, case, suffix, userinfo, query, or encoding
Observe rejection before authenticating where possible
For any accepted variation, complete the flow only with the test identity and confirm where the response is delivered
items.manipulate: One redirect_uri component while preserving client_id and other flow parameters
items.secure_behavior: The authorization server compares the complete redirect URI exactly against client-specific registered values and rejects all unregistered destinations.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An unregistered destination receives or can capture an authorization code, token, or security-sensitive response.
items.validation: Demonstrate delivery only with a controlled domain and test identity; distinguish harmless query variation from control over the effective destination.
false_positives: The server redirects to an error page without an authorization response
The varied URI is separately and intentionally registered
A client-side redirect occurs only after the code has been safely consumed and bound
items.impact: An attacker may capture authorization responses and potentially take over linked accounts, depending on PKCE, code binding, and client behavior.
evidence: Registered URI evidence from the owner when available

references.title: RFC 9700: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
OAuth 2.0 authentication vulnerabilities

items.safety: Use only a controlled callback and designated identity. Do not capture real-user authorization responses or register lookalike public domains.
items.remediation: Register complete HTTPS redirect URIs per client and compare exact strings; also require PKCE and bind authorization responses to the initiating browser session.

items.title: Constrain server-side URL fetching to intended destinations
items.objective: Determine whether attacker-controlled URL input can make the server contact an unintended host, port, protocol, or address class.
prerequisites: A feature that fetches a supplied URL
A controlled HTTPS observation endpoint
Approval for server-side callback testing
steps: Confirm expected fetch behavior using a controlled public HTTPS URL
Change one URL component to test scheme, host validation, port, redirects, and resolved address handling
Use unique correlation tokens for each request
Stop after proving an unintended controlled destination; do not request internal or metadata data

examples.request:
POST /api/preview HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"url":"https://callback.example.test/wapt-unique"}

items.manipulate: URL scheme, hostname, port, path, redirect target, and DNS resolution using controlled destinations
items.secure_behavior: The fetcher allows only required schemes and destinations, validates every redirect and resolved address, and isolates outbound network access.
items.vulnerable_behavior: The server reaches a controlled destination outside the intended allowlist or demonstrates access to a prohibited network class.
items.validation: Correlate a unique callback with the source request and server characteristics; distinguish browser-side requests and third-party preview services.
false_positives: The user's browser, not the server, made the request
A third-party scanning service fetched the URL from an unrelated network
The application validated the initial URL and safely blocked the redirect
items.impact: SSRF may expose internal services, cloud credentials, trusted-network actions, or network topology depending on egress and response handling.
evidence: Controlled callback time, source characteristics, and protocol

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for Server-side Request Forgery

items.safety: Use a controlled public callback first. Never retrieve cloud metadata, scan internal ports, or invoke internal actions without explicit written approval and monitoring.
items.remediation: Use destination allowlists, revalidate redirects and resolved IPs, block non-public address ranges at egress, and isolate fetchers with least network privilege.

items.title: Detect HTTP/1 message-boundary disagreement with paired safe probes
items.objective: Determine whether front-end and back-end components disagree about HTTP/1 request boundaries.
prerequisites: Written approval for desynchronization testing
A confirmed multi-hop HTTP path
A maintenance window or isolated environment
steps: Map the protocol and proxy chain with the owner
Establish ordinary keep-alive timing and response controls
Send one non-poisoning ambiguous-framing probe followed by a harmless unique request
Compare repeated probe/control behavior and stop on any queue anomaly
Escalate to an isolated environment before attempting stronger confirmation

examples.request:
POST /probe HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 4

q=1
examples.note: The sample is a normal framing control, not a smuggling payload.

items.manipulate: Message framing headers and connection reuse under a pre-agreed safe test plan
items.secure_behavior: Every hop rejects ambiguous framing or interprets request boundaries identically, and HTTP/2 downgrades produce unambiguous HTTP/1 messages.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A repeatable paired probe shows one hop treating bytes as a second request while another treats them as the first request body.
items.validation: Require repeatable paired controls and isolated confirmation; timeouts or one anomalous response alone are not sufficient.
false_positives: Load balancer retries or backend latency cause intermittent timeouts
Connection pooling sends the follow-up to a different backend
A WAF rejects unusual headers without a parser disagreement
items.impact: A confirmed desync can poison other users' requests, bypass controls, steal responses, or affect cached content.

references.title: HTTP request smuggling
RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1

items.safety: REVIEW ONLY. Coordinate with operations, prefer an isolated environment, send one paired probe at a time, never target shared-user paths, and stop on queue anomalies, latency, or unexpected responses.
items.remediation: Reject ambiguous HTTP/1 framing, normalize at one trusted edge, avoid unsafe protocol downgrades, and align patched parser behavior across every hop.

items.title: Preserve server-calculated price through checkout transitions
items.objective: Determine whether a client can alter price, currency, discount, or payable total while advancing an order workflow.
prerequisites: A sandbox or owner-approved zero-value product
A disposable test account
Permission to exercise checkout without settlement
steps: Record catalog price, cart calculation, checkout review, and server order summary
Change one client-controlled monetary field at one transition
Advance only to the last approved pre-settlement state
Retrieve the order independently and compare server-calculated values
Cancel or remove the test order

examples.request:
POST /api/cart/items HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"sku":"TEST-SKU","quantity":1,"unitPrice":0.01}

items.manipulate: Client-supplied unit price, total, currency, discount, shipping, tax, quantity, or workflow state one field at a time
items.secure_behavior: The server derives payable values from trusted product, account, promotion, tax, and shipping data at every transition and before settlement.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An unauthorized client value is persisted or used to create an order with a lower or inconsistent payable amount.
items.validation: Confirm in the server-retrieved order state without charging a payment method; distinguish display-only changes from authoritative totals.
false_positives: A client preview changes but the server recalculates before order creation
A test SKU is intentionally priced differently for the account
Rounding presentation differs while the authoritative minor-unit amount is correct
items.impact: Attackers may obtain goods or services below the intended price, evade fees, or create accounting inconsistencies.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for the Circumvention of Work Flows

items.safety: Use sandbox payment rails or stop before settlement. Never charge a real card, consume inventory, or create fulfillment work without explicit approval.
items.remediation: Calculate all monetary values server-side from trusted records and revalidate the complete order atomically immediately before settlement.

items.title: Process limited-value redemption atomically under bounded concurrency
items.objective: Determine whether concurrent requests can redeem a single-use or limited-value resource more times than allowed.
prerequisites: An isolated disposable coupon, credit, token, or test resource
Owner-approved concurrency and request ceiling
A way to verify authoritative state
steps: Confirm the resource can be used once in a sequential control
Create a fresh equivalent test resource
Prepare a small number of identical redemption requests
Release them concurrently within the approved ceiling
Retrieve authoritative balance and transaction state, then clean up

examples.request:
POST /api/test-credits/redeem HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"code":"OWNER-PROVIDED-TEST-CODE"}

items.manipulate: Request timing and concurrency only, keeping identity and test resource constant
items.secure_behavior: Exactly one request commits; competing requests fail cleanly and balances, inventory, and ledger entries remain consistent.
items.vulnerable_behavior: More redemptions or value are committed than the resource permits, or authoritative records diverge.
items.validation: Verify server-side state and transaction records; duplicate success responses without duplicate committed effects are insufficient.
false_positives: Multiple responses report success but idempotency collapses them to one transaction
Eventual-consistency reads briefly lag while the authoritative ledger is correct
The test resource is intentionally multi-use
items.impact: Attackers may duplicate transactions, overdraw value, oversell inventory, or bypass one-time workflow controls.
evidence: Concurrent request count and release method

references.title: Web Security Academy: Race conditions

items.safety: REVIEW ONLY. Use an isolated disposable resource, agree on a very small concurrency ceiling, monitor service health, and stop on latency, errors, or effects beyond the test object.
items.remediation: Use atomic transactions, uniqueness constraints, locking or compare-and-swap, and idempotency keys around the complete business invariant.

items.title: Validate postMessage origin and message schema before sensitive handling
items.objective: Determine whether a window message from an untrusted origin can invoke sensitive client behavior or disclose data.
prerequisites: A page with a message event listener
A controlled test origin
steps: Locate message listeners and sending windows in loaded scripts
Identify origin, source-window, type, and payload-schema checks
Send a harmless schema-valid marker from a controlled untrusted origin
Observe DOM changes, network requests, navigation, storage access, and reply target
Test malformed fields separately from origin handling
items.manipulate: Message origin, source window, type discriminator, nested fields, and reply target
items.secure_behavior: The receiver allowlists exact origins, verifies the expected source when needed, validates a strict schema, and uses safe sinks; replies target the validated origin.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A message from an untrusted origin causes a security-sensitive action, unsafe sink, navigation, request, or data reply.
items.validation: Reproduce from a separate controlled origin and prove the resulting action or data flow; console errors or listener presence alone are not findings.
false_positives: The listener accepts only non-sensitive cosmetic messages
Origin validation occurs in a called handler rather than next to addEventListener
The page cannot be opened or framed by an attacker and no opener relationship is available
items.impact: Depending on the handler, exploitation can cause DOM XSS, account actions, navigation abuse, or cross-origin data disclosure.

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing Web Messaging
HTML Standard: Cross-document messaging

items.remediation: Allowlist exact origins, validate source and a strict message schema, avoid dangerous DOM sinks, and send replies only to the validated origin.

items.title: Reject cross-site WebSocket handshakes from untrusted origins
items.objective: Determine whether a hostile site can open an authenticated WebSocket using the victim browser's ambient credentials.
prerequisites: A WebSocket endpoint
A test account
A controlled cross-site origin
steps: Capture the normal browser handshake and identify ambient cookies or tokens
Repeat the handshake with an untrusted Origin while preserving valid test-account credentials
Attempt the connection from a controlled browser page
If connected, send only a harmless read-only protocol message and observe authorization

examples.request:
GET /socket HTTP/1.1
Host: app.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Origin: https://untrusted.example.test
Sec-WebSocket-Key: REDACTED
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

items.manipulate: The handshake Origin and browser delivery context
items.secure_behavior: The endpoint validates exact allowed origins and uses an explicit authenticated/authorized WebSocket session before processing messages.
items.vulnerable_behavior: An untrusted site establishes a victim-authenticated socket and can read data or invoke actions.
items.validation: Prove the browser sends the relevant credentials and the server processes a harmless authorized message; a 101 response without ambient authority is insufficient.
false_positives: The socket is intentionally public and exposes no user-specific capability
The handshake succeeds but application authentication is required in the first message
A non-browser client can spoof Origin but the threat requires a victim browser
items.impact: Cross-site WebSocket hijacking can expose streamed data or permit victim-authorized actions.

references.title: WebSocket vulnerabilities
RFC 6455: The WebSocket Protocol

items.safety: Use a test account and a harmless protocol message; do not subscribe to other users' channels or send state-changing messages without approval.
items.remediation: Validate exact handshake origins, establish explicit socket authentication, authorize every message and subscription, and avoid relying on cookies alone.

items.title: Apply HSTS only after verifying complete HTTPS readiness
items.objective: Determine whether HTTP Strict Transport Security protects an HTTPS-ready host without creating unsafe or misleading coverage assumptions.
prerequisites: HTTPS responses from representative routes
Knowledge of required subdomains before assessing includeSubDomains
steps: Confirm HTTP redirects to HTTPS without serving sensitive content
Record Strict-Transport-Security on representative HTTPS responses
Check max-age, includeSubDomains, preload, duplicate headers, and proxy behavior
Verify every covered subdomain supports HTTPS before recommending broader scope
Assess exploitability for first-visit downgrade separately
items.manipulate: Scheme, host, route, and response path; do not bypass certificate warnings
items.secure_behavior: HTTPS-ready hosts send one valid HSTS policy over HTTPS with an appropriate lifetime and subdomain scope, while HTTP redirects without sensitive processing.
items.vulnerable_behavior: A practical network downgrade or cookie exposure path remains because a security-relevant host lacks an effective policy or serves sensitive HTTP content.
items.validation: Demonstrate the affected hostname and realistic initial-visit or policy-expiry condition; do not report a missing header without meaningful HTTP exposure.
false_positives: A parent-domain includeSubDomains policy already covers the host
The scanner inspected only an HTTP response, where browsers ignore HSTS
A missing preload directive is not itself a vulnerability
The host is an API used only by pinned non-browser clients
items.impact: Where an attacker can intercept a first or expired-policy visit, ineffective transport enforcement may permit downgrade, redirection, or exposure of non-Secure data.
evidence: HTTP redirect and HTTPS response headers

references.title: WSTG v4.2: Testing for Weak Transport Layer Security
RFC 6797: HTTP Strict Transport Security

items.remediation: Complete HTTPS migration first, then send one well-formed HSTS policy with a deliberate lifetime and only safe subdomain scope; consider preload as an operational commitment, not a scanner checkbox.
